## Summary of action
For the next 4–8 weeks keep a fixed wake time, cut your time in bed to a short sleep window (start ~5 hours), get up if awake >20 minutes, limit naps, avoid caffeine after 14:00 and alcohol within 4 hours, and raise the bed head and avoid late meals to reduce reflux.

## What your sleep points to
Your study showed short sleep (TST 269.5 minutes), very low sleep efficiency (SE 55.9%), absent REM on this night, and mild breathing events (AHI 14.7 events/hour). Watch and try to prevent: **Insomnia** — explains low SE and short TST; **Sleep disorders** — your night shows fragmented, insufficient sleep; **Anxiety disorder** — can make staying asleep harder; **Obesity** — can worsen sleep quality and breathing.

## How the plan addresses these
Keep a fixed wake time every day and initially set time in bed to about 5 hours (so sleep efficiency concentrates into that window); only extend the window by 15–30 minutes each week once SE is consistently ≥85%. Use the bed only for sleep/sex, and if you’re awake >20 minutes get up and do a quiet low-light activity until sleepy, then return to bed. Avoid naps or keep them ≤30 minutes before 15:00. Stop caffeine after 14:00 and avoid alcohol within 4 hours of bed. To limit reflux at night avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime and raise the head of the bed ~6–8 inches. Continue your asthma and GERD medicines as prescribed and bring up persistent night symptoms with your clinician. These behavioural steps (sleep-window restriction, stimulus-control rules, fixed wake time, and sleep-hygiene limits) are effective ways to increase sleep efficiency and improve total sleep time in adults with chronic insomnia and disturbed sleep [1][2], and component analyses identify sleep restriction and stimulus control as key active elements [3].
